This approach has many parallels to "The Machinery of Freedom" by David Friedman

Users are able to create lists of things. Things in this context would be lists of comments and links at a minimum.
But this concept could work for any form of media.

These sets are then joined as either a union or intersection (user preference?) leading to the creation of a blacklist of content.

These blacklists are necessarily public in order for people to be able to apply them to their own view of content. This provides a counterbalance to the censorship associated with traditional moderation.

This approach could be prototyped with voat's or reddit's API.

It's a very rough idea right now, probably easier coded than described.
Distributed Moderation: A proposal for moderation within a crypto-anarchy

Sounds great in concept. Comes across as 𝕋 ∪ ℙ or 𝕋 ∩ ℙ where 𝕋 is the totality of posts, and ℙ is the collective user-preference filter, subsequently sorted by perhaps category, votes, timeliness, relevance (search), etc.

Devil's Advocate points/questions:

  • To keep 𝕋 from being gamed, it would need to be distributed/partitioned across numerous nodes. These would likely need to be encrypted and/or otherwise served blind for full effectiveness. Clients would by necessity be able to receive data from servers, and sniff their stacks and/or use mostly-closed filtering to identify source vs. the set of posts served, on a per-source basis, so with the inevitable unfortunate contraband material being posted, end-users would still potentially face liability for hosting said information, even on a link-only basis.
  • The "invited" vs. "broadcast" issue: In the US anyway, and at my last understanding, over-the-air vs. cable (invited signal) regulations already make it legal, or at least not illegal to distribute content over cable with far fewer restrictions than broadcast signals; this is why e.g. Seattle Public Access in years past was able to host bondage and so forth. People have long had the ability to control their consumption of invited signals (i.e. change the fucking channel vs. "unwillingly" receiving signals they didn't ask for with broadcast). With a distributed, decentralized network, it's harder to nail down, but the same whiny fuckers will complain even if they can control their consumption with their own hand-written blacklists, just as they do on twitter today, despite having the ability to block others. Probably a moot point.
  • Synchronization/propagation: The length of time for posts to propagate across the entire network, but this is more a scaling issue. Lessons from Freenet's failures will likely serve well here.

Really interesting and intriguing idea, with seemingly surmountable hurdles.

My thinking on these lines is to have supernodeish web socket servers that would serve as blind relays between web app clients using end to end encryption.

In terms of propagation I think combining twitter's propagation style with the reddit style presentation could be an interesting approach.

Voting up something would host it (longer?) and voting down or reporting it would delete it and not propagate it.

This would lead to something akin to freenode's model of content falling off the network.

Falling off the network would be possible without enough replication, but something akin to magnet links (in concept, not necessarily in implementation) to store "permanent" references to posts would be ideal -- though of course these still need serving eventually.

A nice-to-have would be a client functionality requirement for clients to replicate & propagate "posts" while they are open, as opposed to a BT-like difference between trackers & clients, but this could be easily tweaked given the likelihood/necessity of an open source requirement for trust.

The user filter would need to be able to be stored/retrievable, but I guess that wouldn't be too difficult. It'd be more ideal if it could be stored in a similar fashion as posts to avoid needing to upload potentially "incriminating" (politically or otherwise) filter sets, but this would make "user accounts/settings" as potentially ephemeral as posts.

Initial seeding/bootstrapping is also an issue, and one that rddt accomplished by essentially astroturfing, but would probably be inevitable.

I absolutely want to have clients act as propagation nodes. Basically the web socket relays just serve as a communication channel between clients; WebRTC could be an option as well for a more pure-p2p setup.

I think that there should be no technical distinction between curative lists, and that they should just be lists of identifiers of content.

So as a user you might have a favorite list and a report list, but to outsiders they don't know which is which. They just see your cryptographic identity, signed statements/labels and your lists and from that make their own determinations about what you are doing.

Basically encoding the idea that one persons moderation filter is another person's interesting content. This was a surprising aspect of /r/ModerationLog and even stronger with /r/undelete people actually view the negative curations of some moderators as a positive curation of good content.
